actions: Construct a three-case dated comparison using Fort William/Anishinaabe, Métis Île-à-la-Crosse and Inuvialuit Delta evidence. For EACH, identify what the actual1780–1850source establishes about land, trade, food, learning or community life; then distinguish a genuinely later source-backed colonial school policy/experience and describe a resulting change in family, language, culture or community control. The Métis1776establishment/late1700fur-trade context is period evidence, while Morin’s1950schildhood belongs only to the later comparison.

Introduce the shared assimilation/separation policy context through the already reviewed NCTR historical account, then locate each selected later account precisely. Explain that the policy harmed connections and agency; cultures continued and people actively maintained and renewed them.

Compare a supported continuity and a forced change in each case. Identify who describes the effects and avoid treating every person or First Nation/Métis/Inuit community as identical. Include community-led responses rather than describing Indigenous peoples only as victims.

Transfer to a fresh short attributed dated case: decide which facts establish earlier life, a later policy, its effects and community agency. Do not assume every historic mission/classroom had the same institutional policy or that a modern speaker’s memories are nineteenth-century observations.

actions: Identify several source-backed components of identity in Canada today: distinct continuing First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples/cultural-language connections, particular community relationships to land/agreements, and public historical memory of Black settlement contributions. Explain identities as plural and living, not one fixed national stereotype.

For each selected component, connect an actual studied1780–1850community or agreement with its continuing contribution or effect, distinguishing fact from inference. Examples use the particular treaty histories and continuing community accounts, period land/trade/learning practices with current community-led cultural transmission, and1849–1850Buxton with its present public heritage recognition. A new modern programme is not falsely described as itself founded in1800.

Use the already reviewed renewal protocol to explain a particular disruption→community-led renewal→identity relationship, not merely name a festival or translate a generic English label. Use the existing distinct-FNMI claim to keep peoples and present-day communities distinct. No target-language fluency is inferred.

Transfer: given a fresh attributed current commemoration or cultural project alongside its actual historical case, explain the supported contribution to identity and which causal claim would need more evidence.

For the unchanged distinct-peoples whole claim, hear/read the short accurately attributed Maxime Morin account, identify its named Métis creator and explain that this particular narrative does not describe every Métis person or every Indigenous people. A generic label without this perspective check is insufficient.

limits: The source’s illustrative bilingualism/symbol/sport lists are not converted into an exhaustive compulsory inventory.
